title: Data Quality and Corrections

sections.body: How this site is kept accurate, in numbers, taken from the site's own records each time this page is rebuilt. It shows what each section is built from, how often it is supposed to be rebuilt, when it last was, what is overdue, what could not be verified, and every correction we have made. Nothing here is estimated; a figure that could not be measured on a run says so.

Refresh schedule: how often a page is supposed to be rebuilt from its sources. A news hub is rebuilt daily, a compliance page every 14 days, a company profile every 90 days.

Last checked: the most recent date a page in the section was rebuilt from its sources, reviewed by the editor, or confirmed against a source that had not changed.

Overdue: a page not checked within its refresh schedule. Overdue means we have not re-checked it on time. It does not mean the page is wrong; most overdue pages are unchanged because their sources are unchanged.

Not verified: a fact we could not confirm from a primary source. The page shows it as unverified rather than stating it.

Correction: a published fact we later found to be wrong. Every correction is listed below with what was wrong and what replaced it.

MeasureCountWhat it means
Lawsuits followed from reporting, not a court docket2State court cases have no public docket feed; their developments come from established outlets and are marked as reporting.
AI incidents with no account of what happened0Every report of the incident is paywalled or blocks automated reading, and no database description was available yet.
Cited sources whose text could not be read0The source is cited on an industry page but gets no summary page of its own, because we could not read its text.
Outbound links found broken59Links checked and found dead; each is repaired or replaced on the page that carries it.
Outbound links that refuse automated checking721Sites that block link checkers. These links are not known to be broken; we simply cannot test them automatically.
Outbound links checked and working14254

Every correction to a published fact, newest first. To report an error, email theworldofai@inkboxmail.com; the editorial policy explains how corrections are handled.

DateWhereWhat was wrongWhat it is nowHow we found it
2026-09-29Industry use casesSome pages summarising the sources cited on industry pages described the source instead of informing: one was about a page that returned an error, others about homepages with no AI content, a page belonging to a different organisation, and pages on this site.Those pages were withdrawn and now lead to their industry page. A source summary is published only when the source itself has substance about AI in the industry, and the rest are being reviewed against the same test. The accounting point now cites the Journal of Accountancy's AI coverage in place of the broken AICPA address.Noticed by the editor on the page.
2026-09-28AI incidentsNine incident pages had no account of what happened, because every report of them sits behind a paywall or blocks automated reading.Those pages now carry a summary written from the AI Incident Database's own description, and say so.Noticed by the editor on the page.
2026-09-27LawsuitsThe same watch recorded eight developments from one verdict, including a headline from a low-quality site claiming a $219 billion verdict.Only the Reuters, AP and Engadget reports were kept; the latest development is the AP report of the September 25 verdict.Review of the watch's first night of output.
2026-09-27LawsuitsAn automated news watch attached a report on GEMA's separate case against Suno to GEMA v. OpenAI as a development in the case.The entry was removed. A headline now changes a case page only if it names the defendant and comes from an established outlet.Review of the watch's first night of output.
2026-09-26LawsuitsThe case was added with the docket number and filing date of New Mexico's separate child safety case against Meta.Both fields were removed and are marked as not yet verified against the court record.Checked while building the state court news watch.
2026-09-25AI ObservatoryThe count beside each Observatory section showed 1, the number of pages, instead of the number of records tracked.Each section now shows what it tracks, for example 55 repositories, 16,363 models, 108 companies.Noticed by the editor on the category page.
2026-09-01PeopleAll 58 person profiles were rendered from a template that expected a different record shape: one showed "[object Object]", quick facts were labelled 0 to 3, and sources held in the record were reported as missing.The template was rewritten to the record's actual shape and all 58 profiles were rebuilt; the example profile went from 289 to 859 words of its own content.A site-wide audit of thin pages.

A pipeline rebuilds the site several times a day from its sources. Each page carries its refresh schedule and the date it was last rebuilt; every run lists the pages that are overdue. Outbound links are re-checked in rotation. Automated news watches can only change a page when their source is an established outlet and the report names the subject, and the editor reviews what they change. This page is rebuilt on every run, so its counts are never more than a few hours old.

description: How The World of AI is kept accurate: sources and refresh schedules for 12940 pages, what is overdue or unverified today, and every correction we have made.
